artists.biography:
Otis Ray Redding, Jr. (September 9, 1941 - December 10, 1967) was an American soul singer-songwriter, record producer, arranger, and talent scout. He is considered one of the major figures in soul music and rhythm and blues (R&B), and one of the greatest singers in popular music. His open-throated singing was an influence on other soul singers of the 1960s, and he helped to craft the lean and powerful style of R&B that formed the basis of the Stax Sound. After appearing at the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival, he wrote and recorded "(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay", which became the first posthumous number-one record on both the Billboard Hot 100 and R&B charts after his death in a plane crash. The Dock of the Bay reached number one on UK Albums Chart, becoming the first posthumous album to do so.

Redding was born and raised in the American state of Georgia. At age 15, he left school to support his family by working with Little Richard's backing band, The Upsetters, and by playing talent shows for prize money. In 1958, he joined Johnny Jenkins's band, The Pinetoppers, and toured the Southern United States while serving as driver and musician. An unscheduled appearance on a session led to a turning point in his career. He signed a contract with Stax Records and released his debut album, Pain in My Heart, in 1964. This album produced his first Stax single, "These Arms of Mine".

Although Redding's initial popularity was with African Americans, he later became equally popular among the broader American public. He and his group first played small gigs in the South, then performed at the Whisky a Go Go nightclub, their first concert in the western United States. Internationally, Redding later performed in Paris and London among other venues. Redding's death was devastating for Stax, which was on the verge of bankruptcy. Later Stax discovered that Atlantic Records owned the rights to the entire catalog. Redding received many posthumous accolades, including the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame. Because of his influence on other artists, he received the honorific "King of Soul".

lastfm.wiki_content: Otis Redding's The Soul Album is a significant work in the realm of soul music, released in April 1966. This album marks Redding's fourth studio effort and showcases his unique vocal style alongside a selection of both original songs and covers. The Soul Album features a mix of Redding's own compositions and reinterpretations of songs by notable artists. Key contributors include guitarist Steve Cropper, who co-wrote several tracks and provided guitar work throughout the album. The album includes covers of songs from artists such as: - Sam Cooke ("Chain Gang") - Eddie Floyd ("Everybody Makes a Mistake") - Roy Head ("Treat Her Right") - Smokey Robinson ("It's Growing") Upon its release, the album entered the Billboard LP charts and peaked at number 54 in July 1966. It enjoyed considerable success on the US R&B albums chart, reaching number 3 and remaining on the charts for 28 weeks. The album also made an impact on the pop and rock charts, peaking at number 58. Critics have praised The Soul Album for its energetic performances and Redding's ability to reinterpret existing songs with his distinctive style. Bruce Eder from AllMusic highlighted the album as a collection of "high-energy, sweaty soul performances," emphasizing its blend of original works and covers that feel fresh rather than merely replicated. The album features contributions from several notable musicians: - Vocals: Otis Redding - Keyboards/Piano: Booker T. Jones, Isaac Hayes - Guitar: Steve Cropper - Bass Guitar: Donald Dunn - Drums: Al Jackson Jr. - Brass Section: Wayne Jackson, Sammy Coleman, Gene "Bowlegs" Miller (trumpet); Charles "Packy" Axton, Andrew Love (tenor saxophone); Floyd Newman (baritone saxophone) . Overall, The Soul Album stands as a testament to Otis Redding's artistry and influence in the soul genre, blending powerful vocals with heartfelt songwriting and dynamic arrangements. perplexity.description:
Otis Redding’s The Soul Album is the singer’s fourth studio LP, released in 1966 on Volt, and it captures him at the height of his powers: raw, urgent, and deeply expressive. Built around his commanding voice and the tightly wound Muscle Shoals/Stax-style backing, the album blends hard-driving soul with slower, more wounded ballads, showing both his grit and his vulnerability.

The record is strongest in its emotional range, moving from the simmering ache of “Cigarettes and Coffee” and “Nobody Knows You (When You’re Down and Out)” to the punchier attack of “Scratch My Back” and “634-5789 (Soulsville, U.S.A.).” It was well received as a key part of Redding’s mid-1960s run, reinforcing his status as one of soul music’s defining voices and helping broaden his crossover appeal beyond R&B audiences.
